lead: The subset construction transforms any NFA, even one with ε‑moves, into a DFA that accepts the same language. It exists because DFAs are easier to implement and to reason about. It is used in lexical analyzers, pattern matchers and any tool that needs a deterministic scanner.

blocks.text: The algorithm builds DFA states that are subsets of NFA states. The start DFA state is the ε‑closure of the NFA start state. For each input symbol the algorithm computes the set of NFA states reachable by that symbol and then takes the ε‑closure of that set. A new DFA state is created for each distinct subset that appears.

items: For each DFA state S and each alphabet symbol a, compute move(S,a) = { q | ∃ p∈S, p --a--> q }.
Take ε‑closure(move(S,a)) → new DFA state T.
Add transition S --a--> T. Repeat until no new subsets appear.

blocks.text: ε‑closure(X) = X ∪ { r | ∃ p∈X, p --ε⁺--> r }
blocks.where: X is a set of NFA states; ε‑closure adds all states reachable by any number (zero or more) of ε‑moves.

items: A DFA state may be the empty set ∅. It represents dead computation.
The DFA is complete: every state has a transition for every symbol.

blocks.text: When the NFA contains ε‑moves, the move step must be followed by an ε‑closure. This ensures that the DFA does not miss any NFA state that can be reached without consuming input.
If the NFA has no ε‑moves, ε‑closure(S) = S and the algorithm reduces to the standard subset construction.

The DFA obtained by subset construction accepts exactly the strings accepted by the original NFA. It may have up to 2^n states, where n is the number of NFA states. In practice many subsets are unreachable, so the DFA is often much smaller.
The table shows that the DFA has three states. The start state {p,r} contains the NFA accept state r, therefore it is an accepting DFA state.

examples.question: Given the NFA with states p,q,r, start state p, accept state r, and transitions: p --0--> q, p --ε--> r, q --1--> r, q --0--> q, r --1--> p. Apply subset construction and give the DFA transition table.
steps: Compute ε‑closure(p) = {p,r}. This is the DFA start state S0 = {p,r}.
For symbol 0 from S0: move({p,r},0) = {q}. ε‑closure({q}) = {q}. Create DFA state S1 = {q}.
For symbol 1 from S0: move({p,r},1) = {p}. ε‑closure({p}) = {p,r}. Transition back to S0.
From S1 on 0: move({q},0) = {q}. ε‑closure({q}) = {q}. So S1 --0--> S1.
From S1 on 1: move({q},1) = {r}. ε‑closure({r}) = {p,r}. So S1 --1--> S0.
A dead state ∅ would be added only if some transition were missing; in this example all transitions are defined, so a dead state is not required.
Build the table with states S0={p,r}, S1={q}, and ∅.
examples.answer: The DFA has three states: {p,r} (start, accepting), {q} (non‑accepting) and ∅ (dead). The transition table is shown in the section above.

traps: Leaving out the dead state ∅ makes the DFA incomplete and causes a wrong answer.
Treating ε‑closure as the original set only, forgetting to add reachable ε‑states.
Marking a DFA state as accepting only when it equals the NFA accept state, instead of when it contains any accept state.
Confusing move(S,a) with moveε(S,a); the latter must include the ε‑closure.
Assuming the number of DFA states is always 2^n; many subsets are unreachable.

quiz.q: What is the ε‑closure of a set of NFA states?
quiz.a: It is the set itself together with every state reachable from it by any number of ε‑moves.

quiz.q: Why does the subset construction always produce a complete DFA?
quiz.a: Because for every DFA state (a subset) and every input symbol the algorithm defines a transition to the ε‑closure of the move set, even if that set is empty.

quiz.q: Given an NFA with states {a,b}, start a, accept b, and transitions a --0--> a, a --ε--> b, b --1--> a, construct the DFA start state.
quiz.a: ε‑closure(a) = {a,b}. Thus the DFA start state is {a,b}.

quiz.q: From DFA state {a,b} in the previous question, compute the transition on input 1.
quiz.a: move({a,b},1) = {a} (b --1--> a). ε‑closure({a}) = {a,b}. So the transition leads back to {a,b}.

quiz.q: An NFA has 4 states. Explain why the resulting DFA may have fewer than 16 states.
quiz.a: Only subsets reachable from the start ε‑closure are created. Unreachable subsets are never generated, so the DFA can be smaller than the theoretical maximum of 2^4 = 16.

quiz.q: If an ε‑NFA has no ε‑transitions, how does the subset construction simplify?
quiz.a: ε‑closure(S) = S for any set S, so the algorithm reduces to computing move(S,a) only, without an extra closure step.

quiz.q: What is the name of the algorithm that converts an ε‑NFA to a DFA?
quiz.a: Subset construction (also called the powerset construction).

quiz.q: State one practical use of DFA after subset construction.
quiz.a: Lexical analysis in compilers, where a deterministic scanner matches tokens efficiently.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, subset construction underlies tools such as lex and flex that generate fast tokenizers. Research extends the idea to symbolic automata where transitions are predicates over large alphabets. Recent curricula combine DFA minimization with regular expression engines for better performance.
